proposals.relationship: Walker uses Foucault’s hierarchy of knowledge to explain the exclusion and subordination of Māori knowledge in the Native Schools curriculum.
proposals.evidence_note: Walker’s own 2016 chapter, p. 24, explicitly cites Foucault (1980) for this interpretation. This is one identified conceptual use in a history of colonial schooling; it does not assign the origin of Māori knowledge, the whole chapter, or Walker’s 1990 book to Foucault. The reference on p. 37 prints the title as Knowledge/Power; Foucault’s original volume was not freshly read.
primary_locators: Reclaiming Māori education (2016), p. 24 first paragraph; reference p. 37.

proposals.relationship: Adds and colleagues identify Walker’s use of Gramsci’s paired domination and intellectual-moral leadership to analyse monocultural media and Māori subordination.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicitly mediated by the joint 2005 Broadcasting Standards Authority report, not a claim to have read Walker’s 2002 chapter Māori news is bad news. Peter Adds, Maia Bennett, Meegan Hall, Bernard Kernot, Marie Russell and Tai Walker retain joint credit. Their literature review specifically reports the Gramsci citation and its media argument. Tai Walker is a separate coauthor, not Ranginui Walker. No exact Gramsci passage or edition is inferred.
primary_locators: The Portrayal of Māori and Te Ao Māori in Broadcasting (2005), p. 47, §2.2.3, final paragraph; continuation p. 48 and bibliography p. 140 entry for Ranginui Walker (2002).

proposals.relationship: Byrnes and Coleborne identify Fanon as an intellectual resource for Walker’s counter-history of colonization and analysis of colonial power and resistance.
proposals.evidence_note: This is the explicitly named reading of Giselle Byrnes and Catharine Coleborne in their joint 2011 editorial: p. 8 discusses colonial disavowal, and note 48 names the revised 2004 Ka Whawhai Tonu Mātou and Fanon’s The Wretched of the Earth and Black Skin, White Masks. Walker’s book and these Fanon editions were not freshly read. The 2004 witness is not silently backdated to the 1990 original or treated as the sole origin of Māori historiography.
primary_locators: Editorial Introduction (2011), p. 8 second paragraph; note 48 across pp. 13–14.

proposals.relationship: Linda Tuhiwai Smith uses Walker’s public defense of Māori communities as an example of scholars’ responsibilities toward their people.
proposals.evidence_note: In her own 27 March 2022 conversation, answering advice for young Indigenous people entering activism and academic spaces, Smith moves from scholarly usefulness and community love to Walker’s conduct on radio and in interviews. This is an explicit exemplary resource in her argument about scholarly responsibility, not inferred mentoring, co-membership, or the origin of Decolonizing Methodologies. The organizer’s transcript pp. 8–9 was read; the audiovisual performance was not watched.
primary_locators: A conversation with Professor Linda Tuhiwai Smith (27 March 2022), transcript p. 8 final question/answer and p. 9 opening three paragraphs.
